findings.evidence: The reading fixed the four-word list, and the docs declare and pin the false refusal (corpus case structural-term-priority-tier-is-refused). D164 says the user decides on narrowing if the measured share goes above 8%. Accepted as intended, but worth watching.

findings.evidence: The entry repeats most of D164. A shorter entry that points to D164 would read better.

summary: The candidate adds reading::check_defined_terms as a step! in refusing_check, right after check_environment_reach. It refuses a reading that does not define ladder, rung, tier or layer when the request uses one of them as a whole word in its plain prose. Defining a term means an assumption that starts `Term <word>:` with at least three words of meaning. These are not counted as uses: quoted or backtick spans, fenced code, parenthesised example lists, paths and identifiers, and the lines Athena's own generators write or copy (skipped only when the generator's anchor sentence is present). I ran `cargo test -p athena-core` in this snapshot: 1138 passed, 1 ignored, 0 failed, and refusal_corpus 19/19 passed. I also ran the athena-context brief test, which passed. What the tests show: the recorded 7bf8 request is refused without a definition and accepted with one. A request built by the real root-cause generator, with quoted mentions only, is accepted. 'stepladder', 'delayer' and requests with no structural word are accepted. Replaying the cited jobs gives g6vy to check_outcome_state, 7bf8 to check_defined_terms, and 0wtc to no check. Athena's reverted-fix runs failed. The doc comment, CHANGELOG, D164 and the READING_RULES line say what was asked. All five changed files are on the deliverables list. fmt, clippy and test passed in the recorded CI run. Findings, all minor: the docs do not state the measured replay share (0 of 50 against the declared 3%); generator lines are matched by hard-coded shapes (acknowledged, with a follow-up named); and the fixed word list refuses some technical uses (declared intended and pinned by a test).
